description: I got the local impact award for Houston Last Year
summary:
Kisan AI is a free web app that works right in the browser on any phone. It takes NASA Earth data and turns it into farm advice for small farmers in India, and it does this in their own language. A farmer can pick their field with GPS or just tap on a map. The app pulls together climate and soil wetness numbers, satellite greenness readings, and other layers like soil moisture, rainfall, groundwater, biomass and imagery along with weather forecasts and mandi prices.

It focuses on three main questions. Should I water this week and how much. Is the crop under stress and why. Which crop rotation fits the land water and goals best. I think the part about explaining temperature soil moisture and vegetation indices is important but it feels like it gets a bit messy when datasets are on different grids. It puts them on a common monthly grid and a 250 m grid to spot seasonal changes and stress periods.

Every result comes with some kind of rating. It compares rotations on things like nutrient cycling erosion water use and market income all based on what the farmer cares about most. There is also an interactive map that shows the layers over time and highlights erosion risk or water stress zones. The AI assistant explains everything in nine languages and keeps reminding users to check things in the field and talk to local experts. Some parts of how it weights the priorities still seem unclear to me.
details:
86% of India's farm holdings are under 2 hectares (Agriculture Census 2015-16). These farmers make high-stakes choices about water, crops and soil by eye while the satellite data that could guide them stays hard to reach and read. Kisan AI puts that data in their hands. It can help save groundwater, catch crop stress and encourage rotations that rebuild soil and protect income as the monsoon grows less predictable.

What it does

Kisan AI is a phone-first web app that turns NASA Earth observations into clear explainable decisions for small farmers in India in their own language. A farmer chooses their field (GPS, a tap on the map or a nearby place) and gets three answers:

Water: whether to irrigate this week and roughly how much from the 7-day rain forecast crop water demand (evapotranspiration) and root-zone soil moisture adjusted for the fields soil type.

Crop health: a season timeline from satellite greenness (NDVI) that marks bare, growing, peak and decline periods, flags crop stress explains the likely cause (drier soil than normal, heat or low rain) and states how confident it is.

Crop rotation: three Kharif → Rabi → rotations, compared on eight criteria: soil nutrients, erosion protection organic matter, pest-cycle break, water use, fodder, income (todays mandi prices) and drought safety.

A Map tab shows NASA layers over time with a date slider: MODIS NDVI, SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall, land-surface temperature, Landsat/Sentinel imagery, GRACE groundwater and GEDI biomass. It also maps field-level zones of erosion risk water-stress hotspots and frost-prone low spots. An AI assistant answers questions in nine languages and a Learn tab explains the science in words.

How it works

Data: NASA POWER (30-year climate normals plus daily rain, temperature, root-zone soil wetness and evapotranspiration) NASA MODIS MOD13Q1/MYD13Q1 NDVI at 250 m and NASA GIBS map layers. Supporting data: ISRIC SoilGrids (soil texture, pH, carbon) Open-Meteo forecast and Copernicus elevation data.gov.in mandi prices and OpenStreetMap place lookup.

Data fusion: sources of different resolution (30 m to 300 km daily to static) are lined up on a common monthly grid and a common 250 m grid. Rain and ET are summed, temperature and soil wetness. Each month compared with its 30-year normal.

Analysis: documented rules rather than a black box:

NDVI smoothing and phase detection;

stress-versus-harvest attribution;

anomalies against past years;

a confidence score;


slope-based erosion zones;


a multi-criteria rotation scorer weighted by the farmers own priorities.
The AI assistant explains these results; it does not invent them.
Benefits and intended impact
Fewer unnecessary irrigations, which saves groundwater, electricity and diesel.
Earlier warning of crop stress with a cause to check in the field.
Rotations with legumes. Cover crops that cut fertiliser costs rebuild organic matter and reduce erosion.
Safer price-aware crop choices in years ("what-if" rainfall and temperature sliders).
A shared explainable view of a field for farmers and extension workers (KVKs).

86% Of India's farm holdings are under 2 hectares. Our goal is to give these farmers the satellite insight large farms have at zero data cost. Next we plan a one-season pilot with a krishi vigyan kendra to validate the advice on fields.

Tools and technologies

Languages: JavaScript (Node.js) HTML, CSS.
Server: Node.js with Express deployed on Vercel in the Mumbai region.
Libraries: geotiff.js (reads satellite pixels from cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs) Leaflet (maps) Anthropic SDK (Claude assistant).
Data services: NASA POWER API, Microsoft Planetary Computer (MODIS) NASA GIBS, ISRIC SoilGrids, Open-Meteo data.gov.in OpenStreetMap.
Hardware: none beyond a phone or laptop. It runs in any browser with no install or login.
Testing: 65 automated tests, plus end-to-end checks in a phone- browser.

What makes it creative

It turns variables (NDVI, evapotranspiration, soil-moisture anomaly) into one-sentence decisions a farmer can act on.

It explains why: every stress finding lists its evidence and a confidence level.

It reads a few kilobytes per field, from NASA MODIS data so it is fast and cheap.

It covers both sides of the farm decision: soil health and market income (live mandi prices) in one comparison.

It works in six interface languages with voice input and read-aloud for farmers who find reading difficult.

Factors our team considered

Accessibility: low-end phones, weak connectivity, local languages, low literacy.

Uncertainty: coarse pixels, monsoon clouds, model estimates. The app shows confidence levels. Asks farmers to confirm in the field.

Judgment: the tool supports, not replaces, farmers and local experts. Reminders appear on every result.

Farmer constraints: water labour and machines fodder needs crops to avoid.

Sustainability: free data sources and open, documented code that others can host.

Ai: the assistant is grounded in computed data and told never to invent prices or schemes.

NASA POWER Climatology API – 30-year climate normals, soil wetness, evapotranspiration
NASA POWER Daily API – daily rain, temperature, root-zone soil wetness, evapotranspiration
MERRA-2 Reanalysis (source of NASA POWER meteorology and soil wetness)
NASA GIBS – Global Imagery Browse Services (map layers)
SMAP L4 Root Zone Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP)
GPM IMERG – Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (rainfall)
MODIS/Terra Land Surface Temperature Daily 1km (MOD11A1 v061)
Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS S30 v2.0) – 30 m imagery
GRACE / GRACE-FO JPL Mascon – groundwater and water storage change
GEDI L4B Gridded Aboveground Biomass Density v2.1
